notes.meaning: Jesus reminded the crowd that He had taught openly in the temple courtyard day after day without being arrested. He allowed them to take Him now because the ancient Scriptures had to come true. Everything that happened followed God's holy plan.

At that moment, all of Jesus' disciples abandoned Him and ran away into the night. Their sudden flight fulfilled Jesus' own warning spoken only a few hours earlier, as well as ancient prophecy. In the moment of crisis, their courage gave way to panic.

A young man was following the group with only a linen sheet wrapped around his body. When members of the crowd tried to grab him, he slipped out of the cloth and ran away naked into the dark. This event highlights how violently the arresting mob acted and how terrified everyone was.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many commentators believe this unnamed young man was Mark himself, leaving a quiet personal signature in his Gospel.

notes.meaning: The arresting crowd marched Jesus directly to the high priest's residence. There, the chief priests, elders, and teachers of the law gathered for a night meeting. Together they made up the Sanhedrin, the highest ruling council of the Jewish people.

Peter followed Jesus from a safe distance until he made his way inside the high priest's courtyard. He sat down among the guards and officers to warm himself by their fire. Sitting among Jesus' enemies placed Peter right in the path of temptation.

The council leaders searched eagerly for testimony that could justify putting Jesus to death. They had already decided on His execution before hearing any evidence. Yet despite their efforts, they could find no legal ground to condemn Him.

Many people came forward to tell lies against Jesus, but their stories contradicted one another. Jewish law required at least two witnesses to agree completely before anyone could be sentenced to death. Because the accusers gave clashing accounts, their claims could not be accepted.

After other attempts failed, another group stood up to bring a new charge against Jesus. They were determined to supply testimony that would hold up in the court. Yet their accusations were still built on falsehood.

The accusers claimed Jesus had promised to destroy the physical temple and build a new one in three days without human hands. They twisted words Jesus had spoken years earlier about His own body being raised from the dead. By making Him sound like an enemy of the temple, they hoped to charge Him with a capital crime.

Even on this charge, the witnesses could not make their details match. Their reports differed enough that the judges still had no solid case against Jesus. The leaders' plot to wrap a death sentence in legal process continued to fail.

Seeing that the prosecution had stalled, the high priest stepped forward in the middle of the council to confront Jesus. He demanded to know why Jesus had offered no reply to the charges. He hoped to pressure Jesus into saying something self-incriminating.

Jesus refused to reply and kept total silence, showing that the false claims did not deserve an answer. His quiet dignity fulfilled what the prophet Isaiah had foretold about the suffering servant. Pressed for a case, the high priest asked Him directly if He was the Christ, the Son of God.

Jesus openly declared that He was indeed the Messiah and the Son of God. He warned the council that they would see the Son of Man sitting beside God in power and returning on the clouds of heaven. By these words, Jesus showed that the One they were judging would one day be their Judge.

The high priest tore his clothes in a formal display of religious horror at Jesus' claim. Tearing garments was an official sign that blasphemy, an insult against God's honor, had been spoken. He announced that the court had no further need for witnesses.

The high priest told the council that they had heard the blasphemy from Jesus' own lips and demanded their vote. Under Jewish law, speaking against God's divine glory carried the penalty of death. The council members all agreed that Jesus was guilty and deserved to die.

Some in the gathering began spitting on Jesus and blindfolded His eyes. They struck Him with their fists and mocked Him, telling Him to use prophetic power to say who hit Him. The officers then took charge of Him with slaps across the face.

While Jesus endured abuse upstairs, Peter was down below in the open courtyard of the palace. One of the high priest's servant girls walked by where Peter was sitting. Her arrival started the test of Peter's loyalty.

The servant girl saw Peter sitting close to the fire and looked closely at him in the firelight. She recognized him and said out loud that he had been with Jesus of Nazareth. Her sudden accusation put Peter on the spot in front of the crowd.

Peter denied the charge immediately, claiming he neither knew Jesus nor understood what she was talking about. He walked away from the fire toward the entryway to escape further attention. Right then, a rooster crowed in the distance.

The servant girl spotted Peter again near the entryway and pointed him out to those nearby. She told the bystanders that he was definitely one of Jesus' followers. Peter found himself exposed again before he could get away.

Peter denied the girl's words a second time. A little while later, the bystanders challenged him again, insisting his northern Galilean accent proved he belonged to Jesus' group. The pressure on Peter was becoming impossible to avoid.

In rising fear, Peter began calling down curses on himself and swore under oath that he was telling the truth. He claimed that he did not even know the man they were talking about. His earlier promises to die for Jesus had turned into desperate lies.

As soon as Peter spoke, the rooster crowed a second time. Peter suddenly recalled Jesus' exact words that he would deny his Master three times before the rooster crowed twice. Overcome with deep grief and shame, Peter broke down and wept bitterly.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: An early church interpretation holds that the Greek word means Peter pulled his cloak over his head in shame so he could weep without being seen.
